desc:
prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. You may make any number of trades; a trade is a buy on some day followed by a sell on a strictly later day. You hold at most one share at a time, and each day you may do at most one action (buy or sell), so the next buy is on a day strictly after the previous sell.

Among all plans that reach the maximum possible total profit, find the smallest number of trades. Return the two-element array [maxProfit, fewestTrades]. If no profit is possible, the answer is [0, 0].

[1, 2, 3, 2, 5, 5, 4] -> [5, 2]   (buy 1 sell 3, buy 2 sell 5)
[3, 2, 1]             -> [0, 0]
[1, 3, 2, 4]          -> [4, 2]   (buy 1 sell 3, buy 2 sell 4)
hints: The maximum profit is easy: look at consecutive day differences. How much of each difference can you keep?
A trade that includes a falling day (next price lower than today's) loses money compared to splitting it at that fall. So an optimal trade never spans a drop.

Cut the price line at every drop prices[i] > prices[i+1]. Every resulting piece that contains at least one rise is exactly one trade (buy at its start, sell at its end). Count those pieces and add up the rises.
editorial: Let d[i] = prices[i+1] - prices[i]. The maximum profit is the sum of all positive d[i]: it is an upper bound, and buying before each rise and selling after it achieves it. To hit this value, no trade may include a negative d[i], and every positive one must be covered.

A trade is a block of consecutive differences. Flat steps (d = 0) are harmless, so a block may include them, and neighbouring rises can be merged into a single longer trade. The blocks are therefore separated exactly by the negative differences. Between two drops, the days form a non-decreasing stretch; it needs one trade if it contains at least one rise and none otherwise.

So scan once, add up the positive differences, and count the number of times a rise starts a new stretch (the previous difference was negative, or it is the first difference, and zero-differences before the first rise do not matter). O(n) time and O(1) space.
